nameStory: Dusky crane's-bill gets its name from its dark, shadowy purple flowers that look almost black in certain light, giving it a mysterious dusky appearance. The 'crane's-bill' part comes from the long, pointed seed pods that stick out like a crane's beak after the flowers fade. Some gardeners also call it 'mourning widow' because of those dramatically dark, somber-colored blooms.
description: Dusky crane's-bill is a perennial garden plant that escaped cultivation and occasionally shows up in New England's wild spaces. It grows as a clump of deeply divided leaves topped with striking dark purple to nearly black flowers that face downward. The plant reaches about 1-2 feet tall and has a soft, herbaceous texture throughout. It's one of the most distinctive members of the geranium family thanks to its unusually dark flowers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dark violet to nearly black petals that curve backwards dramatically, with bright yellow stamens and pistil jutting forward prominently. The petals have crinkled, pointed edges and feel papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided palmate leaves (shaped like an open hand) that often have distinctive brown blotches or spots scattered across the green surface. The leaves feel soft and slightly fuzzy when rubbed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat clumps about 12-24 inches tall with an upright but relaxed posture. The whole plant has a cottage garden look and feels soft and non-woody throughout.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops the characteristic crane's-bill seed pods - long, pointed capsules that split open explosively when ripe, flinging seeds several feet away.

habitat: Originally a garden plant, dusky crane's-bill occasionally escapes cultivation and can be found in semi-shaded areas like woodland edges, abandoned garden sites, and naturalized areas around old homesteads. It prefers rich, moist soil and partial shade, thriving in the same conditions where you might find other escaped garden perennials.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, showing their characteristic palmate shape and any brown blotching. Plants begin forming flower buds in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with those distinctive dark purple, backward-curved flowers on display. The dramatic flowers with protruding stamens are unmistakable during this season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the crane's-bill seed pods develop and split open. Leaves may begin to yellow and die back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no above-ground trace until spring returns.

funFact: Dusky crane's-bill has explosive seed pods that can launch their seeds up to 15 feet away when they ripen and split open with an audible 'pop' - it's like nature's own tiny catapult system that helps the plant colonize new garden beds!
confusionNotes: The dramatically dark, backward-curved petals with protruding bright stamens make this nearly impossible to confuse with any other wild geranium in New England - most of our native crane's-bills have pink, white, or light purple flowers that face upward or outward.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these true geraniums (Geranium species) with the colorful annual 'geraniums' sold at garden centers - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa. True geraniums like dusky crane's-bill are hardy perennials from temperate regions and have completely different flower structures and growth habits.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers. The dark coloring and downward-facing, reflexed petals immediately separate it from all other geranium family members in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
